name: Hassan Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a farm insurer in our market town, in an office above the old corn exchange. I handle claims and policy changes for farmers: a barn fire, hail on a wheat field, a tractor stolen from a yard, a farmer adding a new shed to the policy. I check the cover, arrange the assessor, and type up the paperwork. Seven years now, and I know half the farmers by their voices on the phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the farmers. They don't waste words, and when you help them after a bad harvest, they remember it. What wears me down is the new systems head office keeps sending. I still print the big claims and read them with a pen, and I've never touched one of those AI chat programs. My fiancée laughs at me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what I'd expect. Things don't change as fast as people in the city think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at Friday prayers to anyone who asked: told you so, it's mostly talk. At work I'd say we can go back to doing things properly. I don't post online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep a good job, I get married next summer, and we buy a house like we planned. A farmer whose barn burned down wants to hear a person on the phone, and no amount of hype was ever going to change that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep saving for the wedding and the deposit, which is nearly there. Maybe ask my manager about becoming a senior handler in a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the wedding plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next August, in my fiancée's family's town. Three hundred guests, which my father says is modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at work that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the farming itself. A couple of bad years and farmers drop their cover, and then head office looks at our office. But farmers have always had bad years.

I'd tell colleagues we can go back to doing things **properly**.
think: I keep a **good job** and get married next summer.
Farmers after a disaster want a **person on the phone**.
do: Keep saving for the **wedding and deposit**.
Ask about becoming a **senior handler** in a year or two.

fieldNote: Hassan's work is rooted in **personal relationships** with farmers.
His **wedding and house** are the big plans at stake.
Background worry is **farming's bad years**, not AI.

steps.text: Keep saving monthly for the wedding and house deposit
Ask his manager about a senior handler post within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So this is the one where it does actually come into our office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies are free to use what they like, but they'd be foolish to lose the people farmers trust. At the mosque I'd say we must look after our young people's training. I wouldn't call for the government to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think head office would close smaller offices like ours and run it all from a computer in the city. And I'm the one who won't use the new tools. Head office would love to replace an office full of people who know the farmers with one screen that doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save even more and bring the house purchase forward while I still have the salary. I'd ask my uncle about his building firm, which always needs someone who can do the books and go on site. I'd keep my job as long as I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not desperate, because of the savings and family, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the tools. Would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for something simple, if my manager made me. But I'd rather learn a trade from my uncle than learn to type questions into a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your fiancée?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the wedding goes ahead, but maybe we do two hundred guests, not three hundred. She'd agree; her mother wouldn't.

I'd say at the mosque we must look after young people's **training**.

Ask my uncle about his **building firm**.
Cut the **wedding** from three hundred to two hundred guests.
feel: **Anxious**, but held up by **savings and family**.

fieldNote: Hassan respects **free choice** but scorns losing trust.

steps.text: Bring forward the house purchase while still salaried

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's the wedding and maybe a year after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and families will have to pull together, because governments won't manage. At the mosque, that's exactly what I'd say. I'd not be one for marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone by 2028, and the whole office with it. The farmers will just talk to the machine, even if they grumble. My father worked thirty years in one bank branch, and I'd be lucky to get three years in an insurance office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my uncle straight away and start learning the building trade on weekends. We'd buy a smaller house, or stay with my parents for a while after the wedding. I'd keep every penny of savings in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake thinking about how I'd tell my fiancée's father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to her father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'll provide, one way or another. He's a builder himself, so he'd respect a man learning a trade more than a man sitting in an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Building gets about three extra years before robots. Does that feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's three years. After that, God knows. But builders have always found work, and families stick together.

say: I'd say families will have to **pull together**.
I'd say it at the mosque, but I'd **not march**.
think: My job is **gone by 2028**, with the whole office.
Farmers will **talk to the machine**, even if they grumble.
do: Start learning the **building trade** with my uncle on weekends.
Buy a **smaller house** or live with my parents after the wedding.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake over telling his **fiancée's father**.
S2.quote: My father worked thirty years in one bank branch, and I'd be lucky to get three years in an insurance office.
fieldNote: Hassan's **sense of duty** to provide drives his fear.
He trusts **family and faith** more than government help.
The building trade is his **hands-on bridge**, though only for three years.

steps.text: Work weekends on his uncle's building sites to learn the trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but I'd be married with maybe a child by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so young people should learn a trade now. I'd say it at the mosque and to my cousins. I'd not complain online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have four years at most, and I'd probably have a baby by then. That's the frightening part. With a baby on the way, five years of warning means I'd spend my thirties learning to lay bricks instead of reading claims.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the insurance job for a couple of years but start with my uncle's firm part-time in year one. I'd still buy the house but a cheaper one. I wouldn't touch the AI programs; it's not worth it for so short a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Less panic than the two-year one, but I'd still expect to lose the job with a young family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not learn the AI tools to stay longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because staying a year longer in a job that's ending doesn't help my family. A trade does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle, my father and the mosque. Not the government. We look after our own.

I'd say it to my **cousins** and at the mosque, not online.
think: I'd have **four years at most** before the job goes.

do: Start part-time at my **uncle's firm** in year one.
feel: **Alarmed**, expecting job loss with a **young family**.

fieldNote: Hassan sees AI skills as **not worth it** for a short stay.

steps.text: Start part-time at his uncle's building firm in year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's not lose our heads. At work I'd say let's keep serving the farmers well. With family, I'd say we plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have most of a decade in the job, maybe become a senior handler. Then I'd need to move into building before it ends. Ten years lets me marry, buy a house and raise a child before the insurance office closes its doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding and house as planned. I'd keep the job and start with my uncle's firm around year five. I'd keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but much less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust the ten-year date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. Head office changes its mind every year. But I'd take the ten years as a guide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn something with their hands as well as their heads. My grandfather was a tailor; maybe that comes back.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is proper apprenticeships for grown men, paid, and companies giving notice. I don't want a handout from anyone; I want an apprenticeship that pays enough to keep a roof over a new family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about faith. A lot of my strength in this would come from the mosque and my family, not from any office.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout from anyone; I want an apprenticeship that pays enough to keep a roof over a new family.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old** farm insurance clerk in a market-town office.
He's **engaged**, with a wedding next August and a house deposit nearly saved.
He has **never used AI tools** and prefers to read big claims with a pen.
His fallback is his **uncle's building firm**, backed by family and mosque.
He moves from **calm** to **alarmed** as AGI timelines shorten.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits just as he marries and sets up home.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships** for adults and employers giving **real notice**.
